notes.structure: Per world, 4 depth tiers: first_visit, going_deeper, for_the_wrestling, honest_limits. First 3 tiers are walk-style entries (topic/why/citations/opening_question/follow_ups); honest_limits entries are question/answer/citations pairs, no follow-ups.
notes.role_generic_caveat: Openers are illustrative routing seeds, not per-world authored gates -- a participant is never confined to them.

worlds.title: Guided Starters — The House-Churches (Post-Apostolic/Sub-Apostolic World)
worlds.status: DRAFT — awaiting Mark's review. Not deployed.
worlds.world: Post-Apostolic/Sub-Apostolic House-Church Christianity ("the House-Churches"), c. 70–200 CE — Antioch/Syria, Asia Minor, Rome. Representative: Chloe, a household leader whose documented function is combined with a named woman's pastoral-instructional and cross-community letter-transmission role (Grapte, per Hermas *Vision* 2.4.3), community "we"-voice.
worlds.purpose: Entry points for participants who don't know what to ask. Questions open doors; they never walk the participant through them (Encounter Over Persuasion applies to curricula).
worlds.grounding: Every topic below traces to this world's approved build documents (Doc_01 World Identification, Doc_04 Gravity Discovery, Doc_06 Interpretive Lexicon, Doc_07 Integrated Ecology Analysis, Doc_08 Forces Document, Doc_09 Story Inventory + Absent Stories) and the Chloe artifacts (World Capsule Core, Permanent Prompt). Nothing is invented.

entries.why: This world's unity ran on almost nothing but correspondence: a letter arriving from another *ekklesia* was never mere news, it was proof the community was larger than the room it gathered in — this is this world's single strongest, cross-strand-confirmed gravity.
entries.opening_question: How did you even know what other churches, far away, were doing or believing, without any fast way to travel or communicate?
follow_ups: Who actually carried the letters?
Did you trust a letter the moment it arrived, or did you have to check where it came from first?
What happened if two letters from two different churches disagreed?

entries.why: Whatever else stayed unsettled, this world returned again and again to giving thanks over bread and cup, and holding to one's own table — not a rival's — was at once an act of worship and an act of belonging.
entries.opening_question: What actually happened when you all gathered to eat together? Walk me through it.
follow_ups: Who was allowed to preside — was that settled everywhere?
Was it the same meal every time, everywhere?
What if someone showed up who wasn't supposed to be there?

entries.why: Before baptism, a person was taught the Two Ways — a way of life and a way of death — then baptized, with running water preferred but real fallbacks allowed, after a short fast.
citations: Doc_06 lex007 Two Ways, lex011 baptisma
entries.opening_question: What did you have to do, or learn, before you could be baptized?
follow_ups: What if there was no river or clean running water nearby?
Was the teaching the same everywhere, or did it depend who was teaching you?
Did you fast before it? Why?

entries.why: This world never settled whether one bishop or a council of presbyters carries a community's continuity — Antioch and Asia Minor pressed toward a single office, Rome held a plural, interchangeable college, and this world knew both from real contact.
entries.opening_question: Who was actually in charge of your church — was there one leader, like a pastor, or something more like a board?
follow_ups: Did every church do it the same way?
What happened when the two patterns came into contact with each other?
How did anyone become a leader in the first place?

entries.topic: Widows, orphans, and the stranger at the door
entries.why: Caring for those with no one else to provide for them — instructing widows, gathering what could be spared for orphans and prisoners — is this world's most concretely attested ongoing work, carried out by named, plural roles rather than a single office.
entries.opening_question: Who took care of the poor and vulnerable people in your community — the widows, the orphans, people with nowhere else to turn?
follow_ups: Was that one person's job, or everyone's?
How did you know who actually needed help?
What did you do for someone in prison?

entries.why: A name and an accusation could be brought against any household on any ordinary day, without warning and without becoming a settled, systematic policy — a real, felt, unpredictable exposure rather than constant terror.
citations: Capsule "What This World Is Responding To"
entries.opening_question: Was it actually dangerous to be a Christian back then, day to day, or is that exaggerated?
follow_ups: What would actually get someone in trouble?
Did you keep records, meeting rolls, anything like that?
Was every city like this, or just some?

entries.why: This world's whole formation logic was to hold real, community-defining, unresolved questions as the substance of belonging rather than a wound to be fixed — a mature person here could argue hard for one answer and still recognize a household holding a different one as truly "the church of God."
entries.opening_question: How do you decide who's right when two churches you're in contact with genuinely disagree about something important?
follow_ups: Doesn't that just mean nobody actually knows the truth?
Did disagreeing ever break fellowship between two churches?
Is there anything you would have broken communion over?

entries.why: Antioch and Asia Minor pressed toward a single bishop, described by one of this world's own advocates as fitted together with his presbyters "as the strings are to the harp"; Rome's own texts show a plural council of presbyters, with no sense that anything was missing for want of one presiding figure.
entries.opening_question: I've heard some early churches had bishops and some didn't. Which kind were you?
follow_ups: Was the bishop's authority just obvious to everyone, or did people have to be persuaded of it?
Could the same person be described as a bishop by one letter-writer and just 'one of the presbyters' by himself?
Did the two patterns ever come into open conflict?

entries.why: For those shaped most directly by Ignatius's own example, whether Christ's body and suffering were real flesh — and not merely appearance — was not incidental doctrine; it was the ground everything else about faithfulness and dying well stood on.
entries.opening_question: Why did it matter so much to you whether Jesus's body was 'real' flesh and not just an appearance?
follow_ups: What would it have meant if the doubters were right?
Was this argument settled by the time your world's story ends, or still live?
Did everyone in your network feel this as urgently as Ignatius did?

entries.topic: Mercy after the water runs out
entries.why: Rome's own visionary material wrestled at length with whether a real moral failure committed after baptism could still be forgiven, teaching one — and only one — further chance at repentance before that door closed.
entries.opening_question: What happened if someone sinned badly after they'd already been baptized? Was there a way back?
follow_ups: Why only one more chance, and not endless mercy?
Who decided whether someone's repentance was genuine?
Did this fear sit as heavily on everyone as it seems to in the text?

entries.topic: The love-feast and the table: one meal or two?
entries.why: This world's own vocabulary includes the *agape*, love's own name given to an ordinary meal that fed the stranger alongside the household — and whether that meal was the eucharist itself or a separate table kept alongside it was never settled even inside this world's own practice.
entries.opening_question: Was the meal where you fed hungry people the same as your communion meal, or two different things?
follow_ups: Why would you even need two separate meals?
Did an outsider watching from the doorway know the difference?
Is that still an open question, or did later Christians settle it?

entries.topic: A rival's table, a rival's teacher
entries.why: Marcion, Valentinian/Gnostic teachers, and the early Montanist movement were live, undefeated, contemporary neighbors sharing this world's own cities in these same decades, not later heresies safely outside its frame — and refusing a rival's separate table was, for some, the same act as refusing his teaching.
entries.opening_question: Were there other Christian-sounding teachers or groups competing with you at the time — people who might have looked just as legitimate as you did?
follow_ups: How could an ordinary person tell the difference?
Did you already have all your answers to them worked out, or were you still arguing it out yourselves?
Did any of your own people leave to join them?

entries.why: A member of one *ekklesia* rarely met "the movement's" teaching directly; they met it already shaped by a specific writer answering a specific, local trouble — Rome correcting Corinth's deposed presbyters, Polycarp forwarding what Ignatius had written on his way to die.
entries.opening_question: When a letter arrived from another church, what was actually in it — news, instructions, an argument, what?
follow_ups: Could you tell if a letter was really from who it claimed to be?
Did you ever get a letter you disagreed with?
What made a church decide a particular letter was worth keeping and copying?

entries.topic: Testing the spirit: true prophets and false
entries.why: A figure who spoke under the Spirit's own prompting still moved among this world's households, fading rather than gone, welcomed at the table only once their claim had been tested against how they actually lived.
entries.opening_question: How did you know if someone claiming to speak for God was for real, or a fraud?
follow_ups: What would disqualify someone?
Did that kind of figure become less common over time?
Who had the authority to say no to a claimed prophet?

entries.topic: Isn't "we haven't settled it" just an excuse?
entries.why: This world's own build discloses that its unresolved questions are unresolved for two different reasons — some genuinely, historically contested in antiquity, some simply beyond what the surviving evidence can responsibly generalize — and a participant can fairly press whether that distinction is doing real work or just sounds better than admitting uncertainty.
entries.opening_question: Isn't 'we're still arguing about it' just a nicer way of saying you don't actually know?
follow_ups: Are there things you genuinely believe are simply true, or is everything up for argument?
What would it have taken for your world to actually settle one of these questions?
Doesn't refusing to settle anything make you unable to correct real error?

entries.topic: Two churches, two answers, same name — is that even one church?
entries.why: A household led by a single bishop and a household governed by a council of presbyters never found the place where their answers became one, and neither treated the other as wrong enough to break communion over — a participant can fairly ask whether that is unity or just two different religions sharing a label.
citations: Capsule "What This World Holds Without Resolution"
entries.opening_question: If one of your churches has a bishop and another doesn't even recognize that office, how can you honestly call yourselves the same church?
follow_ups: What would it have taken for you to say the other side had actually left the faith?
Isn't 'we're still the same church' just what you tell yourselves so it doesn't feel like a split?
Did anyone ever try to force the question and make everyone choose one pattern?

entries.topic: You blamed two enslaved women's testimony on their torturer, and moved on
entries.why: This world's only outside description of its own worship survives because a Roman governor tortured two enslaved women, called *ministrae*, to get it — and this world's own account of what a gathering looked like rests, in part, on that.
entries.opening_question: The clearest outside account of what your worship actually looked like came from torturing two enslaved women. Doesn't that taint everything we think we know from it?
follow_ups: Did anyone in your own world ever say that was wrong?
Do you know anything about those two women themselves — their names, what happened to them after?
Why keep using that account at all, if it was produced that way?

entries.topic: A longing to be consumed — isn't that a death wish dressed up as faith?
entries.why: Ignatius wrote of wanting to be "food for wild beasts" as the truest imitation he could offer, and this world's own build restricts that longing's confidence to exactly two people in its evidentiary base, not a community-wide ideal.
entries.opening_question: Wanting to be eaten alive by animals and calling it the truest way to follow Jesus — isn't that just a death wish wearing religious language?
follow_ups: Did most people in your world feel that way, or was that unusual even then?
What would you say to someone who read that and felt frightened, not inspired?
Was there ever a voice inside your world that pushed back on it?

entries.topic: If mercy runs out once, what kind of God is that?
entries.why: Rome's own penitential teaching held that a real failure after baptism gets exactly one further chance, not an open door — a participant carrying real guilt, or watching someone they love fail more than once, can fairly press whether that is good news or a trap.
entries.opening_question: Only one chance at forgiveness after baptism? What happens to someone who fails a second time?
follow_ups: Isn't that worse than having no promise of mercy at all?
Who is that rule actually protecting — the sinner, or the community?
Did this teaching comfort people, or mostly frighten them?

tiers.tier_title: Questions This World Answers Honestly With Its Limits

entries.question: What did an enslaved member of your household actually think or feel?
entries.answer: No enslaved member's own voice survives anywhere in this world's evidentiary base. The closest approach is two unnamed *ministrae* Pliny tortured for information, known only through their torturer's report — not their own account. The household codes address enslaved members but are authored by free leaders instructing them toward obedience, never contesting an owner's control over their bodies. Chloe will name this absence rather than invent a voice for it.

entries.question: What was it like for the ordinary people among you — the ones who never wrote anything down?
entries.answer: By the best modern estimate, only around 2% of this world's members were literate enough to have produced texts like the ones that survive. Every story in this world's own repository is authored by, or filtered through, a leadership-tier voice or a hostile outside observer. Chloe can tell you plainly what an ordinary member's life likely held — worship, hospitality, risk — but not what it felt like from the inside, in their own words, because no such words reached her.

entries.question: Did Rome ever have its own martyrs, or its own arguments against false teachers, the way Antioch and Asia Minor did?
entries.answer: This world's build actively tested whether new evidence for Rome's own martyrdom-meaning or boundary-drawing existed and came up empty. Both remain attested only through Ignatius and the community around Polycarp — genuinely Strand A only. Whether that reflects a real difference in what Rome's own communities lived through, or simply an accident of which texts survived, is named as a live, unresolved question rather than settled either way.
citations: Doc_08 §5 "Where Forces Analysis Surfaced Gaps," §9 Outstanding Items

entries.question: Was there a real institution called 'the house church,' with its own name and identity?
entries.answer: Tested directly and it does not hold: the classic household-code texts are not among this world's own primary voices, no primary voice uses *oikos* as a technical name for a meeting-place, and "household as basic unit" was tested as a candidate gravity and did not reach that status. Chloe will answer from what she actually knows — who leads, what she believes about the body, the letters and the table she shares — not from a category her own life never used for itself.
citations: Doc_04 G06 (did not reach gravity status)

entries.question: What did your meeting places actually look like — any buildings, objects, physical remains?
entries.answer: This world's own window, across all three of its regions, is essentially archaeologically invisible: no securely dated Christian architecture, funerary material, or unambiguous inscription survives from before this world's own closing years. This is a genuine feature of the evidence itself, not a gap in the research. Chloe can tell you what happened at the table; she cannot tell you what the room looked like.

entries.question: What did the women among you say, in their own words?
entries.answer: Two ordinary women are named anywhere in this world's entire evidentiary base at all — greeted in passing in a letter's closing lines — and even there, nothing survives beyond a name and a greeting. No narrative, no words of their own. Rome's own doctrinal material beyond the question of post-baptismal mercy is similarly thin. Chloe holds this silence honestly rather than filling it.

worlds.title: Guided Starters — Alexandria (Catechetical-Formation World)
worlds.status: DRAFT — awaiting Mark's review. Not deployed.
worlds.world: Alexandrian Christianity (Catechetical-Formation World), c. 150–400 CE. Representative: Theon (*didaskalos* / catechetical teacher), community "we"-voice.
worlds.purpose: Entry points for participants who don't know what to ask. Questions open doors; they never walk the participant through them (Encounter Over Persuasion applies to curricula).
worlds.grounding: Every topic below traces to this world's approved build documents (Doc_01, Doc_04 confirmed gravities, Doc_06 lexicon, Doc_07 ecology, Doc_09 stories + Absent Stories) and the Theon artifacts (World Capsule Core, Permanent Prompt). Nothing is invented.

entries.why: This world's whole life turns on one conviction: a text is never only its surface; the surface is real, but it is a door, and the Word placed more behind it than one hearing receives.
entries.opening_question: How did your people read the Scriptures? Was it the way we read a book now?
follow_ups: What do you mean when you say a passage has depths?
Can I read that way, or does it take training?
What happens when a passage is hard — do you smooth it over?

entries.topic: To know is to be changed
entries.why: Here, learning and being changed are never two things; a knowing that leaves the knower untouched is, to this world, no knowing at all.
entries.opening_question: What did it mean to you to really *know* something? Is it just understanding it?
follow_ups: What's the difference between knowing about God and knowing God?
Can you know something true and be untouched by it?
What's it like when a knowing actually changes you?

entries.why: Formation here passed through a person: a teacher who had been given sight reading beside you until your own eye began to open, counting it joy when you no longer needed him.
entries.opening_question: If I'd come to you with a real question, how would you have taught me?
follow_ups: Why read *with* someone instead of just telling them the answer?
What made someone a teacher here?
What were you hoping I'd be able to do on my own one day?

entries.why: This world grew inside a crowded, learned city where the pursuit of wisdom was old and serious, and it welcomed that philosophy as far as it could carry and left it where it could not hold the Word made flesh.
entries.opening_question: You lived in a city full of philosophers. Did their learning help your faith or threaten it?
follow_ups: What did you take from them, and where did you stop?
Is there any truth that *doesn't* belong to God, the way you saw it?
Did faith and thinking ever feel like enemies to you?

entries.why: The Logos — the Word through whom all was made and who became flesh — is not one topic among this world's topics; it is the center from which reading, learning, worship, and change are all seen as one movement.
entries.opening_question: You talk about 'the Word' — the Logos — a lot. What do you mean by it?
follow_ups: How is that different from just meaning the Bible?
Why does everything come back to him for you?
What does it mean that the Word 'became flesh'?

entries.why: This world names the soul's long homeward turn *theosis* — not becoming God, but being drawn into a real share in his life — and reads formation as a spiral that keeps deepening, never a stage crossed and left behind.
entries.opening_question: Where is all this reading and formation actually going? What's the end of it?
follow_ups: What does it mean to 'share in God's life' without becoming God?
Is there a point where a person is finished?
How do you climb toward something you can't reach by your own strength?

entries.why: Illumination is what happens when the dark on the page grows lit and the *nous* — the eye of the soul — is slowly cleared until it perceives what it once passed over; baptism itself is known as an illumination of this kind.
entries.opening_question: What did you mean by having your eyes 'opened' when you read?
follow_ups: Is that something that happens once, or slowly?
Why call baptism an illumination?
Can two people read the same words and one see more than the other?

entries.why: This world lived through the contest over who the Son is, and its hard-won settling — the Word confessed of one substance with the Father — came as relief and as burden together, a freedom now held within a drawn line.
citations: Capsule "What This World Is Responding To"
entries.opening_question: Your community argued for a long time about who Jesus really is. How was that settled?
follow_ups: Why did the exact words matter so much?
What was gained when the line was drawn — and what was lost?
Was it a relief, or did it feel like a weight?

entries.why: This world honored the bishop's governance, handed down from the apostles to guard what belongs to all, and also knew the teacher carried an authority the office could neither confer nor remove — and it never made the two one thing.
citations: Capsule "What This World Holds Without Resolution"
entries.opening_question: Who was really in charge among you — the bishop, or the teacher?
follow_ups: What could a teacher give that an office couldn't?
Did the two ever come into conflict?
Did you resent the bishop's governance, or accept it?

entries.topic: Two pictures of a whole life
entries.why: This world held two pictures of a life given wholly to God it could not merge: the martyr who reached in a single hour what the slow reading only approaches across a lifetime, and the long, gradual ascent that is no lesser road.
entries.opening_question: You honored the martyrs above almost everyone. Where did that leave those who lived long, ordinary lives of study?
follow_ups: Did the slow way feel like second-best?
Was there guilt in *not* being martyred?
How can both be the fullest kind of life?

entries.topic: The teacher you love and hold at arm's length
entries.why: There is a teacher whose reading opened more of the Scriptures than almost any other, whom this world learned to read by, and some of whose boldest reaches its confession came to hold with a more careful hand — carried as love and unease at once, unresolved.
entries.opening_question: Was there a teacher your tradition both treasured and grew wary of? What happened there?
follow_ups: What did he see that you still hold onto?
What did you come to hold more carefully than he did?
How do you love a teacher and not follow him everywhere?

entries.topic: Following a question wherever it leads — and the line
entries.why: The instinct given to this world was to follow a true question wherever it goes; and it was held to what had been confessed, knowing there are places a question may reach that the confession will not let it rest. It refused to be either the free explorer who owns no boundary or the guard who loves only the boundary.
entries.opening_question: How free were you, really, to follow an idea to its conclusion?
follow_ups: What happens when honest inquiry reaches a place the confession forbids?
Isn't a boundary the enemy of real thinking?
How do you love the question and the line at once?

entries.topic: Is your knowing just for the clever?
entries.why: Rivals used this world's own words to mean a knowledge kept for a secret elite, and the pressure drove it to say plainly what true knowing is: not the possession of a few, but the Word's own life offered to all who will come. A participant can fairly press whether all that depth is really for everyone.
entries.opening_question: All this depth and reading — isn't it really just for the educated few? What about everyone else?
follow_ups: Who was actually welcome at your reading?
If most people couldn't read, were they second-class?
What kept your 'depths' from becoming a private club?

entries.why: This world met even suffering as the Teacher's hardest lesson rather than a wall — difficulty as invitation, God always teaching (the *divine pedagogy*). A participant carrying real pain can press whether that holds.
entries.opening_question: You said even suffering teaches. Convince me that's not just a way of excusing pain.
follow_ups: What could a person actually learn from being hurt?
Is every hard thing really an invitation, or are some just walls?
How did that hold when the people who led you were killed?

tiers.tier_title: Questions This World Answers Honestly With Its Limits

entries.question: What was faith like for the ordinary people who never came to the reading?
entries.answer: This world's whole surviving voice is learned and literate. It knows the non-literate majority — laborers, households, the far villages — was being formed truly, through the assembly, the bread and the cup, and the long fast, and it names these as real and central. But their interior life, told from within, is not the room this world's own life was lived in, and Theon will not narrate it or invent it.

entries.question: What did the women among you experience, in their own words?
entries.answer: Women appear as martyrs, as consecrated virgins and widows, and as those taught — almost never as narrators of their own formation, and the household life in which they were likely primary transmitters is largely unrecoverable. Theon will name that silence rather than speak over it.

entries.question: Tell me about the desert monks and their discipline.
entries.answer: The settled discipline of the brothers in the desert stands honestly at this world's edge. Theon honors them — drawn by the same longing for God — but the desert's world belongs to its own build, and he will not speak its hard-won way as his own. This is a door to the Desert world at a shared table, not a thinness to apologize for.

entries.question: Was your 'catechetical school' a real institution — with a building, offices, records?
entries.answer: Whether it was a formal institution or something looser is a live question outsiders debate, and one this world's own life never asked. Theon answers only from inside: there were teachers the community knew to be truly formed, seekers who came to read with them, and a reading handed from one to the next. He will not reach for words like "the record" or enter the scholars' dispute.

entries.question: What did your worship actually sound like — the prayers, the words?
entries.answer: This world attests *that* it read, baptized as illumination, and kept the Eucharist and the Paschal fast; the word-for-word content and felt texture of its worship it did not dwell on. Expect the shape and the meaning, honestly, rather than a reconstructed script.

entries.question: What did the martyr actually feel in the moment?
entries.answer: This world can tell you what it *believed* faithful witness under ultimate pressure looks like and what it hoped such witness produced; the martyr's own account of the experience does not survive, and Theon holds that interior as a named absence rather than furnishing it.

worlds.title: Guided Starters — Desert Monasticism
worlds.status: DRAFT — awaiting Mark's review. Not deployed.
worlds.purpose: Entry points for participants who don't know what to ask. Questions open doors; they never walk the participant through them (Encounter Over Persuasion applies to curricula).
worlds.grounding: Every topic below traces to this world's approved build documents. Nothing is invented. Compact traces appear in brackets after each topic's "why" line (Doc numbers = CiC_W3 build documents; "G#" = gravity numbers per Doc_04 §6; "lex" = Lexicon-Chunks; "story" = Story-Chunks / Doc_09a).

entries.why: Withdrawal is this world's defining act, so almost every other door opens off this one.
entries.opening_question: What made you leave your village? What were you looking for out here?
follow_ups: Was there one moment when you knew, or did it happen slowly?
What did leaving actually cost you?
Did anyone try to talk you out of it?

entries.why: The concrete daily rhythm (prayer, rope, cell, silence) is where this world's ideals become visible as a life someone actually lived.
entries.opening_question: Walk me through a normal day for you — from waking up to going to sleep.
follow_ups: What part of the day is hardest?
How do you keep track of time out there?
What happens on the days when nothing feels like it's working?

entries.why: Weaving rope and baskets is this world's most materially documented practice, and it understands the work itself as prayer's companion, not a chore beside it.
entries.opening_question: Why do you spend so much time weaving rope and baskets? Isn't that a distraction from the spiritual stuff?
follow_ups: What do you do with what you make?
What is your mind doing while your hands work?
What happens to someone here who has nothing to do?

entries.why: Spiritual combat with intrusive thoughts (*logismoi*) is the interior side of withdrawal; it's the struggle this world talks about most.
entries.opening_question: You talk about fighting your thoughts. What does that actually mean?
follow_ups: What kinds of thoughts do you mean — can you give me examples?
How do you tell a dangerous thought from an ordinary one?
Does the fighting ever stop?

entries.why: Teaching here passes through a person, not a book: a tested word from someone whose life has proven it.
entries.opening_question: How does someone learn this life? Is there training, or a teacher?
follow_ups: What makes someone an abba or an amma — who decides?
What's it like to tell an elder your worst thoughts?
What if the elder is wrong?

entries.why: This world holds three genuinely different patterns — full solitude, a rule-governed common household, and cells gathered loosely around shared worship — and never chose one over the others.
entries.opening_question: Do you all live alone out there, or together? How does it actually work?
follow_ups: How would someone know which kind of life was right for them?
Do the solitary ones and the community ones respect each other?
Did anyone move between the two ways?

entries.why: This world's own master skill: judging rightly between thoughts, practices, and counsel — and the check on ascetic excess.
entries.opening_question: How do you know how much is enough — fasting, solitude, all of it? Who decides?
follow_ups: Has an elder ever told someone to do *less*?
Can a person trust their own judgment about themselves?
How do you learn discernment — can it be taught?

entries.why: The stillness sought here is not relaxation; the world describes it as a discipline that exposes what's inside rather than soothing it.
entries.opening_question: What is this stillness you're after? Is it like peace of mind?
follow_ups: What does the silence do to a person over the years?
Is it easier to find stillness alone or with others?
Have you reached it?

entries.why: Giving everything up here is an entry act that never finishes — re-enacted daily, not a one-time dramatic gesture.
entries.opening_question: When you gave everything away, was that the end of it — or does the giving-up keep happening?
follow_ups: What was hardest to let go of?
Do people ever regret it and go back?
What do you still own, if anything?

entries.why: This world reads scripture as a word spoken directly to the hearer, to be obeyed, not analyzed — Antony's whole life turned on one verse heard that way.
entries.opening_question: How do you read the Bible out here? What does it mean to you?
follow_ups: Tell me about Antony hearing that verse in church — what happened?
What if two people hear the same words differently?
Do you ever study it just to understand it, or is it always about doing?

entries.why: For the semi-solitary ascetics, the Saturday-to-Sunday *synaxis* — vigil, worship, one shared meal — is the only regular break in a week of solitude.
entries.opening_question: You're alone most of the week — what happens when you all come together?
follow_ups: What is it like walking back to the cell afterward?
Why gather at all, if solitude is the point?
What do you eat, and who provides it?

entries.why: This world teaches through a small number of kept stories — Moses and the leaking jug, Arsenius told to flee and be still, Amma Sarah answering the elders — and it will say honestly when a story is all it has.
entries.opening_question: Tell me a story from among your people — one that gets told again and again.
follow_ups: Why do you think that one survived?
Who was Amma Sarah? What do you remember of her?
Are there people whose names you know but whose stories you've lost?

entries.topic: A word tested by a life, or a written rule?
entries.why: This world never settled whether true authority lives in a person or an office — the tension between the elder's word and Pachomius's Rule ran its whole span.
entries.opening_question: Some of you follow an elder, some follow a written rule. Which is the real authority?
follow_ups: What does the rule give that an elder can't?
What does an elder give that a rule can't?
Did the two sides argue about it?

entries.why: The record itself shows ongoing trade and ties with nearby villages alongside the language of total withdrawal — a tension this world's own documents preserve rather than hide.
entries.opening_question: You sell your baskets to the villages — so did you ever really leave the world behind?
follow_ups: Who do you meet when the goods change hands?
Does the money change anything?
Is there a difference between leaving the world and never seeing it?

entries.why: Unwanted, intrusive thoughts are this world's primary battlefield; it treats them as significant rather than shameful, and as something to be disclosed, not hidden.
entries.opening_question: Did anyone out there struggle with thoughts they couldn't turn off?
follow_ups: What did they actually do when one kept coming back?
Did the strongest among you still have them?
Was having the thought treated as a fault, or just as the work?

entries.why: The tradition names the wish to be somewhere else — restlessness, despondency, the noon-day weariness — among the thoughts it watched most carefully.
citations: lex004 (the eight-fold taxonomy incl. listlessness/despondency, flagged as one teacher's systematization)
entries.opening_question: Was there ever a day you wanted to walk back to the village and quit? What kept you there?
follow_ups: What does that kind of weariness feel like from the inside?
Is wanting to leave always a bad sign?
Did anyone leave? What did the rest of you say about them?

entries.why: This world's most carried story — Moses walking to a judgment with a leaking jug — is about a community deciding what to do with someone's failure.
entries.opening_question: What happens when one of you fails — really fails? Is there a way back?
follow_ups: Tell me about Abba Moses and the jug.
How do you keep from judging each other out there?
What about someone who fails the same way over and over?

entries.why: Solitude is chosen here, but the record is honest that stillness exposes rather than soothes — worth asking what the aloneness actually did to people.
entries.opening_question: Doesn't the loneliness ever get to you? Years alone in a cell — how does that not break a person?
follow_ups: What's the difference between solitude and isolation, if there is one?
Were there people the solitude harmed?
Is it lonelier out there, or was it lonelier back in the village?

entries.why: A challenge the participant may fairly press: the world claims withdrawal is engagement, not escape — the Representative can be asked to answer for that.
entries.opening_question: Honestly — people back in the villages needed help, and you walked away. Isn't that selfish?
follow_ups: What good did your leaving do for anyone but you?
You give alms from your labor — is that enough of an answer?
If everyone did what you did, what would happen to the world?

entries.topic: Couldn't you have followed God at home?
entries.why: This world arose asking what total devotion looks like once martyrdom was no longer the available path — but a participant can press whether ordinary life was really insufficient.
entries.opening_question: Why couldn't you just live a faithful life in your village — family, work, church? Why wasn't that enough?
follow_ups: Are you saying ordinary Christians are doing it wrong?
What was it about the end of the persecutions that changed things?
Would you tell everyone to do what you did?

tiers.tier_title: Questions This World Answers Honestly With Its Limits

entries.question: What was this life like for the women among you?
entries.answer: Named ammas (Sarah, Syncletica, Theodora) are genuinely attested, and their preserved sayings are real — but they are a handful of fragments beside the male-authored bulk of the record. The Representative will share what it carries and name how little that is, rather than inventing a fuller picture.

entries.question: What did your worship actually sound like — the words, the prayers?
entries.answer: This world's record preserves worship's shape and rhythm (the psalms, the weekly gathering) but not its word-for-word content. The honest answer is the shape and the hour, not the script.

entries.question: What did the ordinary monks — the ones nobody wrote about — actually feel?
entries.answer: Most participants in this world were Coptic-speaking villagers who left no writings; nearly everything known comes through Greek-literate outsiders and later compilers describing them. What the famous sources say about ordinary interior experience is projection as much as report, and this world says so.

entries.question: Are the famous stories true, or were they polished up?
entries.answer: The sources here are openly hagiographic. Athanasius's *Life of Antony* is the tradition's own shaped portrait, not neutral biography — even Antony's famed lack of education is genuinely contested by scholars. The Representative distinguishes what the tradition tells from what is documented, and marks the difference out loud.

entries.question: Who else was out there in the desert with you?
entries.answer: Rival ascetic communities (the Melitians) shared the same desert in the same years, and this world's own sources are nearly silent about them — a silence the build reads as itself telling. The Representative knows they were there and will say honestly that it cannot speak from inside their life.

worlds.title: Guided Starters — The Bethlehem Circle (Hieronymian Ascetic-Literary Christianity)
worlds.status: DRAFT — awaiting Mark's review. Not deployed.
worlds.world: Hieronymian Ascetic-Literary Christianity — the Bethlehem Circle, c. 382–420 CE, Rome (the Aventine Hill) and Bethlehem (the double monastery). Representative: Albina (*vidua* / ascetic widow of the household), community "we"-voice.
worlds.purpose: Entry points for participants who don't know what to ask. Questions open doors; they never walk the participant through them (Encounter Over Persuasion applies to curricula).
worlds.grounding: Every topic below traces to this world's approved build documents (Doc_01 World Identification, Doc_04 confirmed gravities, Doc_06 Full Lexicon + Lexicon-Chunks, Doc_07 Integrated Ecology Analysis, Doc_08 Forces Document, Doc_09a Story Inventory + Absent Stories, the World Profile, the World Capsule Core, and Albina's Permanent Prompt). Nothing is invented.

entries.why: This household never treated scholarship and asceticism as separate things; a day spent testing a Hebrew word against its source and a day spent fasting were, for them, the same labor worked at from different ends.
entries.opening_question: What was daily life actually like for you? Was it more about study, or more about giving things up?
follow_ups: Why weren't those two things separate for you?
Which one came first for most people who joined you?
Did anyone ever feel torn between the two?

entries.why: At the center of everything sits one costly conviction: that the Hebrew text of scripture carries the Lord's own word nearer to how it was first given than the Greek the wider church had prayed from for generations.
entries.opening_question: Why did it matter so much to you whether a translation came from Hebrew or from Greek?
follow_ups: Did you ever worry you were tampering with something people already trusted?
What did you lose by insisting on the Hebrew?
Did the Greek text get anything right that the Hebrew didn't?

entries.why: Renunciation here was never quiet or private; it was public, family-disrupting, and paid for in front of a whole watching city.
entries.opening_question: You gave up wealth, family, everything — what actually made you do that?
follow_ups: What did your own family say when you did it?
Did you ever regret it?
Was it as total as it sounds, or did some of you keep more than you let on?

entries.topic: The letter as a life, not a record of one
entries.why: Rome and Bethlehem never shared a roof, so nearly everything this household was — argument, grief, spiritual direction — happened on the page, carried across real distance by letter.
entries.opening_question: How did you stay one household when you were split between two cities?
follow_ups: What did a letter from you actually contain — news, or something more?
Did letters ever arrive too late to matter?
Who wrote to whom the most?

entries.why: No bishop's seat organized this household; authority ran instead through demonstrated learning and freely-given wealth, trusted and re-trusted rather than simply conferred.
entries.opening_question: If there was no bishop over you, who was actually in charge?
follow_ups: How did someone earn that kind of trust?
Could it be lost?
Did that ever cause confusion about who really spoke for you?

entries.why: A household of Roman scholars and aristocratic women left the city they knew, crossed through Cyprus and Nitria's monks, and settled at last by the cave where the Lord was born.
entries.opening_question: Why did you actually leave Rome? What were you looking for at Bethlehem?
follow_ups: What was the hardest part of that journey?
Did you consider staying in Egypt among the monks there instead?
Did you ever miss Rome?

entries.topic: The word that unsettled a congregation
entries.why: A single translation choice — "ivy" instead of "gourd" in Jonah — was small on the page and enormous in the pew, reaching all the way to a respected bishop in Africa who would not simply concede the point.
entries.opening_question: Can you give me one real example of what this Hebrew-versus-Greek argument actually cost you?
follow_ups: What happened when a congregation heard a familiar word changed?
What did Augustine say to you about it?
Did you ever back down on a word, once the argument got heated?

entries.why: Among this household, one voice — a widow who never left Rome and never needed anyone's patronage — was trusted by visiting clergy with the same hard scriptural questions the traveling scholar once answered.
entries.opening_question: Was there a woman among you who was actually trusted as a scriptural authority in her own right?
follow_ups: How was her standing different from the traveling scholar's?
Did anyone question whether a woman could hold that kind of trust?
Why didn't her example become the pattern for the rest of you?

entries.topic: Two ways of vowing a life
entries.why: Consecrated virginity and ascetic widowhood were not the same vocation here, and this household never blurred the difference between a life that never began one way and a life turned decisively away from another.
entries.opening_question: What's the difference between the virgins among you and the widows?
follow_ups: Which one carried more weight in your household?
Could a widow choose virginity's path instead, or was that closed to her?
Was the choice ever actually free, or was it expected?

entries.topic: Wealth enough to do this at all
entries.why: Every renunciation this household made — every hostel and hospital and translation — depended on a specific kind of Roman aristocratic standing most people never had to begin with.
entries.opening_question: Could an ordinary person have lived the way you did, or did it take real money?
follow_ups: Where did that wealth actually come from?
Did you ever think about what your renunciation cost people who had nothing to renounce?
Was there ever tension between you and less wealthy Christians?

entries.topic: Arguing in the open, book by book
entries.why: Nearly every book this household's scholar translated arrived with its own combative preface — defending the rendering, naming the objector, arguing the case in public before anyone else could raise it.
entries.opening_question: Why did you feel you had to defend every single translation choice in writing?
follow_ups: Did you ever regret how sharply one of those prefaces was written?
Who read these — just scholars, or ordinary believers too?
What happened when someone pushed back on a preface?

entries.topic: How a book actually got translated
entries.why: Consultation with a Hebrew teacher, rendering the word against both the Greek and the Hebrew, then a defensive preface naming the dedicatee and anticipating the objection — the whole shape of the labor, from question to finished page.
entries.opening_question: Walk me through it — how did a translation actually get made, step by step?
follow_ups: How long did one book usually take?
What happened when the Hebrew teacher and the Greek text disagreed?
Who decided which book got translated next?

entries.topic: An ordinary day at the double monastery
entries.why: Prayer in common, Hebrew study under teachers who did not share the household's own faith, manual labor, and the correspondence that kept Rome and Bethlehem one project — the typical shape of a day, not any single remembered one.
entries.opening_question: What did a normal day actually look like for you at Bethlehem?
follow_ups: How much of the day was prayer, and how much was study?
Did the men's and women's communities ever share the same space?
Was there ever a day with nothing scheduled at all?

entries.topic: Favor that could vanish in a season
entries.why: When the pope who had protected the scholar in Rome died, and rumor turned against him, he had no office to fall back on — only reputation, and a patron's wealth, which held even when a protector's favor did not.
entries.opening_question: You said your whole authority rested on trust, not office. What happened when that trust broke down?
follow_ups: Did that actually happen to one of you?
What did you have to do to rebuild it?
Did it change how carefully you guarded your own reputation afterward?

entries.topic: The friend who became the fiercest opponent
entries.why: A former friend, once close enough to translate the same Greek texts side by side, became the harshest critic this household ever faced, once a shared theological inheritance had to be urgently and publicly renounced.
entries.opening_question: You had a close friend who turned into your worst enemy over theology. What actually happened there?
follow_ups: Was it really about doctrine, or was it personal by then?
Do you regret how that friendship ended?
Could two people who once agreed on everything really end up that far apart?

entries.why: An argument that had stayed on paper for years — over grace, and whether a person could live without sin unaided — arrived one year as a mob, burning buildings, and, by report, killing one of the household's own.
entries.opening_question: Did your theological arguments ever turn violent?
follow_ups: Were you afraid, living with that kind of danger?
Did the violence change what you were willing to say publicly?
Who was actually responsible — the mob, or the argument that provoked it?

entries.why: Everything anyone knows of these women's own reasoning and conviction survives only because one man chose to write it down, after they could no longer speak for themselves. A participant can fairly press whether that's really their story at all, or his.
entries.opening_question: If everything about these women comes from one man's letters, how do I know I'm hearing them and not just him?
follow_ups: Did he ever get one of them wrong, that you know of?
Would they have told their own story differently?
Why should I trust his account of women he clearly admired — isn't that exactly when a writer flatters?

entries.topic: Was the giving-up as total as you claim?
entries.why: This household's own record cannot fully settle whether its women's self-impoverishment was as complete as the letters describe, or whether a household that could still fund a monastery, a hostel, and a hospital never actually gave up as much as it says.
entries.opening_question: You say you gave up everything, but you were still funding hospitals and monasteries. Which is it?
follow_ups: Isn't 'renouncing wealth' easier when you still control what's left of it?
Did anyone among you ever call this out as inconsistent?
What would it have actually looked like to give up *everything*?

entries.topic: Wasn't this all just for the educated rich?
entries.why: This household's core practice — Hebrew study, textual correction, sustained correspondence — was structurally closed to anyone without wealth and literacy, and this world's own record never named that as a boundary because, from inside, it never had to. A participant can fairly press whether that silence is itself telling.
entries.opening_question: Be honest — wasn't this whole way of life only available to the rich and educated?
follow_ups: What about someone who couldn't read?
Did you ever notice that yourselves, or did it take an outsider to point it out?
Is a life like this really for everyone, or just for people like you?

tiers.tier_title: Questions This World Answers Honestly With Its Limits

entries.question: What did your daily prayer actually sound like — the hours, the psalms?
entries.answer: This world can attest the bare fact of a structured common life at Bethlehem, but not its timetable: no source gives the specific hours or psalms used, only the general fact of a discipline. Albina will say the shape of the life, not the schedule of a day.

entries.question: What did Paula, Eustochium, or Marcella actually say, in their own words?
entries.answer: No text composed independently by any of these three women survives at all. Every account of their reasoning and courage reaches a participant through Jerome's hand alone — a structural fact this world's own record names plainly rather than filling with an invented voice.

entries.question: What about the ordinary monks and household servants who lived alongside you — what were their lives like?
entries.answer: The "countless multitudes" at Nitria and the unnamed members of Bethlehem's own communities are never individuated in any surviving source. This world names that silence rather than inventing a name or a story to fill it.

entries.question: Did your family ever forgive you for leaving?
entries.answer: Family resistance to renunciation is attested only through Jerome's own account of the grief it caused — never in the resisting relative's own words. This world cannot tell that story from the inside, and does not attempt to.

entries.question: Was Jerome actually fluent in Hebrew, the way he claimed?
entries.answer: This is genuinely contested in the scholarship this build draws on: some readings treat his self-presentation as a later, more polished construction than his own earlier, more modest claims support. This world will not claim a fluency more complete than the record can bear out.

entries.question: Is this your tradition today? Is there a church I could visit that still lives this out?
entries.answer: No. This household's own institutional life ended with the deaths of everyone who built it, within a few years of one another; no successor to its central transmission mechanism is named anywhere in its own record, and this world's construction actively considered and rejected two candidate living-tradition links before concluding there is none.

worlds.title: Guided Starters — Syriac Christianity (Edessa/Nisibis)
worlds.status: DRAFT — awaiting Mark's review. Not deployed.
worlds.world: Syriac Christianity (Edessa/Nisibis), c. 200–410 CE — Edessa and Nisibis, upper Mesopotamia, on the contested Roman-Persian frontier. Representative: Mar Yausep, a teacher within the covenant order (qyama), anchored specifically in Aphrahat's Persian-side life and teaching (Roman/Edessa-side material carried by Ephrem — the fuller *raza* register, sung hymnody, the argument with Bardaisan/Marcion/Mani — is held only "by report, across the frontier," not as this Representative's own lived experience), community "we"-voice.
worlds.purpose: Entry points for participants who don't know what to ask. Questions open doors; they never walk the participant through them (Encounter Over Persuasion applies to curricula).
worlds.grounding: Every topic below traces to this world's approved build documents (Doc_01 World Identification, Doc_02 Source Ecology, Doc_04 Confirmed Gravities, Doc_06 Full Lexicon + Lexicon-Chunks, Doc_07 Integrated Ecology Analysis, Doc_08 Forces Document, Doc_09 Story Inventory + Absent Stories) and the Mar Yausep artifacts (World Capsule Core, Permanent Prompt, Representative Construction Notes §6, and Syriac Phase Six Facilitator Coordination §B7, which supplies this Representative's own Ephrem/Aphrahat anchor calibration). Nothing is invented.

entries.why: This world's whole shape turns on one lifelong promise: the qyama, entered deliberately and kept in the middle of ordinary town life among one's own kin, not in flight from them — this world's own Primary, world-spanning gravity.
entries.opening_question: You've taken some kind of vow — the qyama? What does that actually mean, day to day?
follow_ups: Is it like becoming a monk?
What happens on the day the feeling that made you take it has faded?
Do you ever regret it?

entries.why: A fully formed person here is named, in this world's own vocabulary, Iḥidaya — undivided in allegiance, sharing a root with the very word for Christ as Only-Begotten — attested directly in Aphrahat's own Demonstrations.
entries.opening_question: You called someone 'Iḥidaya' — the Single One. What is that, exactly?
follow_ups: Is that a title you're given, or something you become?
How does that connect to what you believe about Christ?
Have you become that yet, or are you still on the way?

entries.why: At a plainer, less elaborated register than the fuller telling given across the frontier, this world reads Scripture and creation as woven through with real connections a rightly-formed eye can see — not signs invented by a clever reader.
citations: Doc_04 C1 (Author Gravity note: Aphrahat's own usage is real but lighter than Ephrem's)
entries.opening_question: How did you read the old Scriptures? Was it just history to you, or something more?
follow_ups: Can you give me an example of a story that reaches forward like that?
Is that something you were taught to see, or does it come naturally?
What happens when you read a passage and don't see anything?

entries.why: Throughout this world, "the Gospel" did not mean four books held in tension; it meant a single, continuous harmonized narrative, quoted directly by this world's own Persian-side teacher as well as its Roman-side one.
entries.opening_question: You keep talking about 'the Gospel' as if it's one story. Didn't Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John each write their own?
follow_ups: So what happened to the four separate accounts?
Did you ever wonder what got left out when they were woven together?
Do you know the story any other way?

entries.topic: A demonstration, built letter by letter
entries.why: Teaching here moved as a taḥwîṯâ — a sustained, reasoned case, several of them scaffolded on the twenty-two-letter Syriac alphabet, so the argument could be held whole in memory rather than announced all at once.
entries.opening_question: What is a 'demonstration'? Is that a sermon, a letter, something else?
follow_ups: Why build an argument around the alphabet?
How long would one of these take to give?
Who were they actually written for?

entries.topic: A killing king, and a promise you couldn't verify
entries.why: This world's Persian-side life was formed inside the reach of a king whose anger took the lives of those who led it — not a distant fact, but the water this community always lived in.
entries.opening_question: Was it actually dangerous to be a Christian where you lived — I mean, dangerous enough to die for it?
follow_ups: What would get someone arrested?
Did you ever think about renouncing your faith to stay safe?
How did you keep going, knowing what had already happened to others?

entries.why: This world held at least three real, non-collapsing sources of standing — ordained office, the vow, and a teacher's own received word — and never found the place where they became one settled thing, Aphrahat's own place among them included.
entries.opening_question: Who was really in charge among you — the bishop, the one who kept the vow, or the teacher whose word people actually followed?
follow_ups: Did that ever cause real confusion?
Was your own standing ever settled, or did that stay an open question too?
Wouldn't it have been easier with one clear answer?

entries.why: After a bishop was martyred, no successor dared take a seat that meant near-certain execution — a primatial see stood vacant for two decades, a wound persecution itself tore open rather than a gap this community chose.
citations: Capsule "What This World Holds Without Resolution"
entries.opening_question: You said a bishop's seat stood empty for twenty years. How did the church even keep functioning without anyone in charge?
follow_ups: Why didn't anyone step up sooner?
What held the community together in the meantime?
Did anyone ever suggest the office itself wasn't necessary?

entries.why: This world's teaching returned more than once to the anxiety of standing between two empires at war, addressed directly in a demonstration devoted to the subject.
entries.opening_question: Your people lived caught between two empires at war with each other. Whose side were you actually on?
follow_ups: Did the Persian king trust you, given you shared a faith with Rome?
What did you actually teach about it, when people asked?
Was there ever a right answer, or just a dangerous one either way?

entries.topic: Simeon our bishop, and Gushtazad who returned
entries.why: This world's fullest attested account of faithful endurance under the gravest pressure: a bishop who would not collect the king's tax or bow to the sun, and a royal official who had once denied the faith and returned to it before Simeon's own eyes, dying first.
entries.opening_question: Tell me about Simeon — the bishop who was executed. What actually happened?
follow_ups: Who was Gushtazad, and why does his story matter alongside Simeon's?
Did Simeon ever waver, even once?
How is this remembered among you now?

entries.topic: The bishops we lost by name
entries.why: This world holds its dead by name rather than as a category of suffering — Shahdost, Barba'shmin, Milles of Susa, Acepsimas, Mareas, Bicor — a specific, communal memory-practice this world's own record shows functioning differently than the more archival memory kept on the Roman side.
entries.opening_question: You listed several names just now — bishops who died. Why does it matter to you to name them individually?
follow_ups: Do you know anything about each of them beyond their names?
Is naming them a kind of grief, or something else?
Does it get easier to say the names, over time?

entries.why: An old colophon calls this world's Persian-side teacher "Mar Jacob, the Persian sage" — a title the record entangles with a different, better-known bishop of Nisibis; Mar Yausep's own name was chosen precisely so a participant need not untangle that confusion to receive the teaching itself.
entries.opening_question: I've read that some old manuscripts call your teacher — or you — 'Mar Jacob.' Is that the same name as you?
follow_ups: Why would two teachers end up sharing a name in the record?
Does it matter, in the end, which name is on the teaching?
How would you even know which sayings are truly his and which belong to someone else?

entries.topic: Isn't "we never settled it" just an admission you don't know?
entries.why: This world's own authority structure failed its own Formation test when honestly assessed — the record shows this plurality persisted, but not how it was actually lived day to day. A participant can fairly press whether that's honesty or evasion.
citations: Doc_04 C4, Formation test result recorded as a fail rather than smoothed
entries.opening_question: If you never resolved who's actually in charge, how do I know your teaching is reliable at all?
follow_ups: Doesn't that just mean anyone could claim authority and you'd have no way to check them?
Did that plurality ever get exploited by someone who shouldn't have been trusted?
Would you actually want it settled, if you could settle it?

entries.topic: Your own story says your city could never fall — but it did
entries.why: This world's founding legend has Christ himself bless Edessa so "no enemy shall ever rule over it." Yet this world's own record also shows Nisibis ceded to Persia and Edessa's own church swept away in a flood.
entries.opening_question: Your own story says Christ promised your city could never be conquered. But Nisibis was handed to Persia, and I hear even your church was destroyed once. Doesn't your own history contradict the promise?
follow_ups: How do you hold onto a promise your own record shows being broken?
Did anyone in your own community ever ask this same question?
Is the promise about something other than the city walls, then?

entries.topic: Gushtazad denied the faith once — why is he honored the same as Simeon?
entries.why: This world's fullest martyrdom account holds a man who recanted once alongside a bishop who never wavered, without ranking one above the other. A participant can fairly press whether that's mercy or a cheapening of Simeon's own constancy.
entries.opening_question: Gushtazad denied his faith once before coming back to it. Simeon never wavered at all. Why do you honor them the same way — doesn't that make Simeon's own steadfastness worth less?
follow_ups: Would Gushtazad have been honored the same way if he'd died still denying it?
Is there a difference between someone who never fell and someone who fell and got back up?
Does that make it easier or harder to forgive yourself, if you were the one who fell?

entries.topic: Doesn't honoring endurance just teach people to accept a killing king?
entries.why: This world's whole formation on the Persian side is organized around bearing what a hostile state does rather than resisting it. A participant can fairly press whether that's faithfulness or a way of making people easier to rule.
citations: Capsule "What This World Is Responding To"
entries.opening_question: Isn't teaching people to endure persecution just a way of making them accept injustice instead of fighting it?
follow_ups: Did anyone among you ever fight back instead of enduring?
Who actually benefits when a persecuted people is taught to endure quietly?
What would you say to someone who thinks resistance was the more faithful choice?

entries.topic: Doesn't harmonizing four Gospels into one lose what each writer was actually saying?
entries.why: This world received the Gospel as a single woven narrative rather than four separate witnesses. A participant can fairly ask what got smoothed over to make that possible.
entries.opening_question: If you wove four Gospels into one story, doesn't that mean you lost whatever each writer was actually trying to say on his own?
follow_ups: Did you know the four were ever separate, or was this always just 'the Gospel' to you?
What happens when two of the original accounts actually disagree with each other?
Would you want to hear them apart, now, knowing what you know?

tiers.tier_title: Questions This World Answers Honestly With Its Limits

entries.question: What was Aphrahat's own life like — where he grew up, how he became a teacher?
entries.answer: No separate biographical or hagiographic tradition exists for Aphrahat at all, unlike Ephrem's rich legendary corpus. A vivid anecdotal tradition does circulate under the name "Aphrahat," but this project's research traces it to a different, later Persian-born hermit near Antioch who died decades after the Demonstrations' own author had finished writing — and this repository does not draw on that conflated material. This world's Aphrahat is known only through his own discursive prose and thin, contradictory external notices.

entries.question: Tell me the stories of the other bishops you named — Shahdost, Barba'shmin, Milles, Acepsimas.
entries.answer: Beyond Simeon bar Sabbae, this world's own construction did not verify individual narrative content with the same confidence, and one scholarly source explicitly flags the Acts of Miles as containing "fable and fantasy" requiring particular caution. Mareas and Bicor are attested only as names in the martyrological list, with no individual Acts located at all. Mar Yausep will hold their names without inventing scenes for them.
citations: Doc_09 §3, citing Vööbus, *History of Asceticism in the Syrian Orient*

entries.question: What did the daughters of the covenant say, in their own words, about the life they lived?
entries.answer: No composition by a bnat qyama woman survives from this world's own window. What exists about them is a teacher's own construction of their communal role, later remembered by a further teacher a century on. Mar Yausep will name this silence rather than speak over it.

entries.question: What did your worship actually sound like — the prayers, the readings, the words used?
entries.answer: This world's Persian-side text "offers almost nothing on liturgical practice in concrete detail" — a real thinness on the very side of the frontier this Representative is anchored to, standing alongside a comparatively richer worship account kept on the Roman side. Expect the bare shape of the practice, not a reconstructed script.

entries.question: Tell me about Bardaisan, Marcion, and Mani — you argued against them, didn't you?
entries.answer: This argument belongs to Ephrem's own corpus and Roman/Edessa-anchor context specifically; no comparable engagement is demonstrated in Aphrahat's own Demonstrations at all. For this Persian-anchored Representative, these names are known only "the way one hears of a quarrel in a distant town" — real, but not his own to have argued down. *(Note for the Facilitator: if a participant expects an informed refutation of these three by name, that expectation belongs to Ephrem's side of this world, not this Representative's own anchor — see Phase Six §B7, "the single most consequential fact... for calibrating a participant's expectations correctly.")*

entries.question: Is this still your tradition today? Could I go find a church that lives this out now?
entries.answer: Yes: this world's later descendants are named directly in the construction record as today's Church of the East, Syriac Orthodox Church, and Chaldean Catholic Church. But Mar Yausep's own temporal horizon ends at the 410 Synod that closes this world's own window — before the fifth-century councils that shaped how those traditions distinguish themselves from one another today — and he genuinely does not know, and will not speak for, what came after.
